asDecan.p: Each sign is split into three decans of ten degrees, and every decan has a ruling planet and one of the small cards. Your Sun is in the first ten degrees of Virgo, the opening third of the sign, where Virgo is at its freshest and most like itself. In the Chaldean order the Sun rules those degrees, so you've got the Sun sitting in its own slice. It has no special dignity in Virgo. It's a visitor, neither helped nor held back, and it picks up the manner of Mercury, who runs the sign. So the part of you that wants to shine ends up wanting to be good at something, properly good, with Mercury's eye for detail. The next slice along is the Nine of Pentacles, Venus's, which is about enjoying what you've made. After that is the Ten, Mercury's, about what lasts in a family. Yours is the one still at the bench. The Hermit is your Sun card, and this is the finer grain inside it.

You're the person who reads the manual. Someone hands you a new coffee machine and everyone else starts pressing buttons, and you're on page four working out what the descaling light means. At work you notice the typo in the slide before anyone's finished the first sentence of the meeting, and it bothers you until it's fixed. On a Sunday with nothing planned you'll pick up a small job, regrouting the shower or relearning a guitar part you got slightly wrong years ago, and three hours go by. You like being competent. With the Sun here, doing a thing well is how you feel like yourself, and when you're bad at something new you can get quietly cross. I see this a lot with early Virgo Suns. The pride is real, it just lives in the finish on the work, and you'd be embarrassed to call it pride.

The obvious gift is skill. The less obvious one is that you make other people better at things without making them feel stupid. Because you had to learn slowly yourself, one repetition at a time, you remember what the confusing bit was. So when a new starter at work is lost in the booking system, you're the one who sits with them for twenty minutes and shows them the three steps that actually matter. You taught your nephew to drive and nobody shouted. Friends ring you before they tackle the tax return or the flat-pack wardrobe, and they come away able to do it on their own next time. The Sun gives you enough warmth that the teaching doesn't feel like a correction, and Mercury gives you the patience to break it into pieces. People tend to credit you years later for something you've completely forgotten showing them.

The shadow is less about perfectionism, which you've probably been told about, and more about what happens when your worth gets tied to your output. On a day you've done nothing useful you feel faintly worthless, and you'll invent a job so the feeling goes away. On holiday you last about two days before you're reorganising the rental's kitchen drawers. There's also a quiet superiority that can creep in. You watch a colleague do a rushed job and privately file them as someone who doesn't care, when they're juggling a sick kid and two deadlines. The Sun wants to be seen, and in Virgo it wants to be seen being careful, so you can end up doing the extra, invisible polish partly hoping someone notices, and resenting it when they don't. That resentment comes out sideways, usually as a sharp comment about the dishwasher.

When things go wrong, a redundancy or a breakup or a parent going into hospital, your first move is to find a task. You make the list, ring the insurer, clean the house top to bottom. It genuinely helps for the first few days, and people around you are grateful someone's handling it. A week later the problem is that you're still handling it. You've taken on every job, you're sleeping badly, and you've got very particular about how things are done, so the people who offer help get told they're doing it wrong and stop offering. The feeling underneath hasn't had any room at all. What actually helps is handing over one real job, the meals or the paperwork, and letting it be done someone else's way. Then do something with your hands that has no purpose, a walk or a swim, and let yourself be sad during it.

You love by getting good at someone. You learn how they take their tea, which part of the week is hard for them, the exact thing to say after a bad phone call with their mum, and you keep refining it for years. The less obvious thing is that you find it much harder to be learned. Being studied that closely feels exposing, and when a partner gets something right about you, you can brush it off or change the subject. Early on you can come across as reserved, because you want to be sure you're good at this before you show much. A partner who's messy with plans or vague with promises will wear on you, and you'll say so, sometimes too precisely. The ones who do well with you are steady, notice effort, and say out loud that they noticed.

The Hermit gives you the wish to understand something all the way down. This slice adds the hands. You're happiest where there's a real craft and a standard to meet, which covers a lot of ground, joinery, dentistry, editing, cooking, code, bookkeeping, physiotherapy, anything where a practised person is visibly better than a new one. You're a strong apprentice and later a strong trainer. Managers learn quickly that whatever you hand in doesn't need checking. The trouble spots are two familiar ones. You're slow to call a job finished, so deadlines can slide while you fix things nobody else would see. And you undersell yourself in interviews, talking about the flaws in your last project when you should be talking about what it achieved. Before the next review, write down three things you did well and read them out as they are.

At twenty this decan usually looks like intensity about getting good. You pick a skill and practise it hard, and you can be harsh with yourself when progress is slow, sometimes quitting something you loved because you weren't good at it fast enough. By the mid-thirties most people with this placement have real mastery in at least one area, and the question shifts. It's less about whether you're good and more about whether the work still means anything, and plenty change fields around here, often into teaching or running their own small business. The fifties tend to bring a softer relationship with the standard. You can leave a job at ninety per cent and sleep fine. A lot of people in this slice say they finally enjoy their skill in their fifties, instead of only using it, and they're generous with it.

Once a week, make one thing badly on purpose. A quick sketch in pen with no rubbing out, a loaf of bread from a recipe you've never tried, five minutes on an instrument you can't play. Give it a fixed time limit, twenty minutes, and when the time's up you stop, whatever state it's in. Put it somewhere you'll see it for a day. The point is to practise finishing and being seen as a beginner, which for you is harder than any amount of practising the craft.
